direct_answer: When frailty is advanced or someone is nearing the end of life, the focus often shifts to comfort. Joint pain can be eased with positioning, gentle movement, pressure care and suitable medicines. Palliative care teams, GPs and community nurses can help, and care planning makes wishes clear.

content:
Arthritis pain still matters when cure is not the goal. Comfort and dignity come first.

This guide covers comfort-focused care for joint pain. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Comfort and positioning

  • Change position regularly, with help if needed.
  • Use pillows to support painful joints.
  • Pressure-relieving mattresses and cushions may help.
  • Gentle movement can ease stiffness.

Pain relief

Medicines may be adjusted to focus on comfort. Your GP or palliative care team can advise. Tell them about side effects such as drowsiness or constipation.

Planning care

Advance care planning lets you record what matters to you and where you would like to be cared for.

Support for carers

Community nurses, hospices and carers' services can support families.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is palliative care only for cancer?

No, it is for anyone with a life-limiting illness.

Can care be at home?

Often yes; discuss it with your GP.
